1.text:
Are We Alone?

We've traveled from Earth to the Solar System, to the Sun, to the stars, to galaxies, and all the way to the beginning of the universe. Now we end with the biggest question people have ever asked.

Are we alone, and how would we know? In this deck, you'll learn how astronomers find planets around other stars, where life could survive, how a telescope can sniff a planet's air from trillions of miles away, and why nobody has found aliens yet.

2.text:
Today I Can...

This is your checklist. Copy these as "I can" statements and rate yourself at the end.

I can define an exoplanet and tell how the first ones were found. I can explain how a transit reveals a planet's size. I can explain how a star's wobble reveals an unseen planet. I can describe direct imaging, microlensing and rogue planets. I can flowchart how a planetary system, hot Jupiter included, forms. I can explain why the habitable zone moves with star type. I can judge whether TRAPPIST-1 and Proxima b could hold life.

I can read a Webb spectrum for the gases in a planet's air. I can model how life changes a planet's air and spot false alarms. I can compare Mars, Europa, Enceladus and Titan as places to look. I can use the Drake equation as a model and discuss the Fermi paradox. And I can connect today's question to the whole course. These connect to Indiana standards ES.2.2, ES.1.1, ES.2.1 and ES.4.1, plus some enrichment.

3.text:
Worlds Around Other Stars

An exoplanet is a planet that orbits a star other than the Sun. For most of history, nobody knew if they even existed.

In 1995, astronomers found the first exoplanet around a normal star like ours. The star is 51 Pegasi, a Sun-like star. Its planet, 51 Peg b, makes one orbit every 4.2 days. For scale, Mercury's orbit takes 88 days. So this giant planet is hugging its star far closer than Mercury hugs the Sun.

Did you know? The discoverers, Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz, shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics.

4.text:
How Many Have We Found?

Since 1995, the count has exploded. As of October 2026, the NASA Exoplanet Archive lists more than 6,400 confirmed exoplanets (6,451 when checked on Oct 31, 2026).

Here are the planets found by each method. Transit found 4,785. Radial velocity found 1,204. Microlensing found 292. Direct imaging found 98. Other ways found 72. You'll learn the top four methods in the next few slides.

Did you know? The count grows almost every week, so the real number is probably higher by the time you read this.

5.text:
A Tiny Dip in Starlight

A transit is a planet crossing in front of its star, which dims the star a little. It's like a moth flying in front of a porch light.

Follow the three moments. 1: the planet is beside the star, and the star is at full brightness. 2: the planet starts to cross. 3: the planet is fully in front, and the brightness dips. On the graph of brightness over time, the transit shows up as a little dip.

The dip depth tells you the planet's size: dip depth = (Rp ÷ Rs)², where Rp is the planet's radius and Rs is the star's radius. A bigger planet blocks more light. And the time between dips tells you the planet's year.

6.text:
Jupiter vs. Earth in Front of the Sun

How big is the dip? A Jupiter-size planet blocks about 1% of the Sun's light. That's a deep dip.

Earth is a lot smaller. An Earth-size planet gives a dip of only about 0.008%, barely a wiggle. That's about 120 times shallower than Jupiter's dip.

That's why finding Earth-size planets needed super-precise telescopes in space. On the slide, the Earth dot is drawn 2.5 times too big, just so you can see it.

7.text:
A Wobbling Star Gives a Planet Away

A planet doesn't just orbit its star. The star and planet both orbit their center of mass. Because the star is so much heavier, it only wobbles in a small circle.

We can't see that tiny wobble directly, but we can detect it with the Doppler effect. When the star moves toward us, its light shows a blueshift. When it moves away, it shows a redshift. That's radial velocity: a star's speed toward or away from us, read from Doppler shifts in its spectrum.

It's the same physics you used in Deck 19 for galaxy redshifts. But here the shifts go back and forth, over and over, with the planet's orbit.

Did you know? Jupiter makes the Sun wobble at about 13 m/s, about 30 mph, once every 12 years.

8.text:
Seeing Planets, Even Ones with No Star

Sometimes we can photograph planets directly. In direct imaging, the star's glare is blocked so the faint planet can be seen. Around HR 8799, there are 4 young giants. Young planets are still warm, so they glow in infrared light.

Another method is microlensing. A star's gravity bends and brightens a far star behind it, just like the lensing you saw in Deck 18. If a planet orbits the lens star, it adds a short spike to the brightening.

One more twist: a spike all alone means a rogue planet: a planet drifting through space with no star to orbit. Some planets don't belong to any solar system at all.

9.text:
Flowchart: Building Another Solar System

You built a flowchart of how our Solar System formed in Decks 4 and 16. Now you'll show the same theory building a planetary system around another star. This task matches standard ES.2.1.

Draw five boxes: 1, the cloud collapses, and a star and disk form. 2, dust sticks into planetesimals, then protoplanets. 3, rocky planets form inside the frost line, with ice-rich cores outside. 4, big cores pull in H and He, forming Jovian planets, with moons. 5, a giant spirals inward and becomes a hot Jupiter, like 51 Peg b.

Draw each step with the star at the left. Label leftover asteroids and comets in box 5. Draw the frost line in box 3 (Deck 4 Slide 10), and label what made the giant move inward in box 5. Last line: why can't a giant planet form right next to its star?

10.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 1

Read the light curve like an astronomer. A star dims by 1% every 3 days. What is most likely going on?

Is it A) a Jupiter-size planet orbits it every 3 days, B) an Earth-size planet orbits it every 3 days, C) the star is moving away from us, or D) a rogue planet drifts past once? Use Slides 5 to 8 and choose.

11.text:
Not Too Hot, Not Too Cold

The habitable zone is the distances from a star where a planet's surface could hold liquid water. Too close, and it's too hot: water boils away. Too far, and it's too cold: water freezes. It's sometimes called the Goldilocks zone.

The zone moves with star type. Around a hot F star, the zone is far out. Around the Sun, a G star, it's about 1 to 1.7 AU, and Earth sits right inside it. Around a red dwarf, an M star, the zone hugs the star.

Why? Brighter stars pour out more energy, so you need to be farther away to keep cool. Dim stars give off less, so you need to snuggle in close.

12.text:
TRAPPIST-1: Seven Earth-Size Worlds

TRAPPIST-1 has 7 Earth-size planets around one red dwarf. They're named b, c, d, e, f, g and h.

The star is so dim that all seven planets crowd in close, much closer than Mercury is to the Sun. Even so, e, f and g are in the habitable zone.

That makes TRAPPIST-1 one of the best places to search for life outside the Solar System.

Did you know? TRAPPIST-1 is about 40 light-years away, and each planet's year lasts just 1.5 to 18.8 days.

13.text:
What Does "Earth-Like" Mean?

When the news calls a planet "Earth-like," it usually just means about Earth's size, not Earth's air, water or life.

Take Proxima b, which has about Earth's mass. It orbits our nearest neighbor star, in its habitable zone. What we know: its mass (at least), its orbit, and the starlight it gets. What we don't know: does it have air? Water? Life?

There's also a problem. Its star blasts out flares and X-rays, which could strip away air. "Earth-like" is a long way from "Earth."

Did you know? Proxima b is about 4.2 light-years away, the closest exoplanet we know of.

14.text:
A Zoo of Strange Worlds

Most planets we've found are nothing like home! Here are some of the strangest.

Hot Jupiters orbit their star closer than Mercury orbits the Sun. Leaking hot Neptunes sit close in, losing gas into space. Lava worlds have about a 1-day year and are hot enough to melt their surfaces. Mini-Neptunes are 1.7 to 4 × Earth wide, bigger than Earth but smaller than Neptune.

Why are these so common in our lists? Big planets close to their stars are the easiest to find with transits and wobbles.

15.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 2

Think carefully about what the habitable zone really tells us. A planet orbits in its star's habitable zone. What do we know for sure?

Is it A) its surface could hold liquid water, if its air is right, B) it has living things on it, C) it is covered in oceans, or D) it is the same size as Earth? Use Slides 11 and 13 to decide.

16.text:
Webb Sniffs a Planet's Air

When a planet transits, a little starlight passes through the thin ring of air around its edge on its way to Webb. Each gas absorbs its own wavelengths, its fingerprint from Deck 15.

A transmission spectrum is starlight filtered through a planet's air while the planet transits. On the graph, the higher the line, the more light blocked at that wavelength, measured in microns from 3 to 5.

In 2022, Webb looked at the giant planet WASP-39b. There was a CO2 hill at 4.1 to 4.6 microns. That was the first clear detection of carbon dioxide on a planet outside our solar system.

17.text:
Gases That Life Leaves Behind

A biosignature is a sign, such as a mix of gases, that life may be making. On Earth, life changes our air all the time.

O2 (oxygen) comes from plants and microbes. CH4 (methane) comes from microbes. These two gases destroy each other over time, so finding them together means something keeps making both. O2 + CH4 together are hard to explain without life.

But astronomers must be careful. Some non-living processes can make these gases too, so every possible explanation has to be ruled out.

18.text:
Has Anyone Found Alien Life?

So far, there are 0 confirmed signs of life beyond Earth. But there has been a lively debate.

K2-18b is 2.6 Earths wide and 124 ly away. The claim: in 2023 and 2025, the Madhusudhan team reported hints of DMS, a possible life gas. The replies: 2025 re-checks by the Luque, Schmidt and Stevenson teams found no significant DMS.

This is how science works. One team makes a claim, other teams check it, and the case stays open until the evidence is strong.

19.text:
Capstone Model: Could It Hold Life?

It's your turn to be an astrobiologist. This task matches standard ES.4.1. Draw two panels: A, Earth's air and its cycles. B, my exoplanet's air. Pick a planet card: TRAPPIST-1e, Proxima b or K2-18b.

Draw both atmospheres. Show the gases (N2, O2, CO2, H2O, CH4), where they sit (layers, ozone) and how air circulates. Add arrows for gas swaps with life, oceans, rocks and industry (Deck 11 Slide 5).

Finally, circle the gas Webb should look for, and one way it could fool us.

20.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 3

Think like a careful scientist. Webb finds O2 in a planet's air. Is that proof of life?

Is it A) not yet, because starlight can also make O2 with no life, B) yes, because only living things make O2, C) yes, if the planet is in the habitable zone, or D) no, because telescopes can't detect gases at all? Use Slides 16 and 17 to decide.

21.text:
Life at the Extremes

What life needs is pretty simple: liquid water, energy (light or chemicals), and the elements C, H, N, O, P and S (carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus and sulfur).

But life is tougher than you'd think. Look at the thermometer. Water freezes at 0 °C, and water boils at sea level at 100 °C. Yet a deep-sea microbe still grows at 122 °C! At the cold end, microbes have been seen growing at about -15 °C, and some still show signs of life at -25 °C.

Living things that survive in conditions like these are called extremophiles. If life can survive here, it might survive in harsh places on other worlds.

Did you know? Deep-sea vent microbes live in total darkness, getting their energy from chemicals instead of sunlight.

22.text:
Where to Look Next Door

Astrobiology is the study of where life came from, how it changes and where else it could be. And some of the best places to look are in our own Solar System.

Mars has old lakes and rivers, so it may once have held life. Europa, a moon of Jupiter, has a salty ocean under ice. Enceladus, a moon of Saturn, has plumes that spray out its ocean into space. Titan, Saturn's largest moon, has methane lakes and an organic haze.

Did you know? Europa's hidden ocean may hold about twice as much water as all of Earth's oceans.

23.text:
The Drake Equation Is a Model

In 1961, Frank Drake wrote an equation to estimate how many civilizations might be out there: N = R* × fp × ne × fl × fi × fc × L. N is the number of civilizations in our galaxy we could detect.

Each factor is one step. R* is new stars per year (measured). fp is stars with planets (measured). ne is planets that could hold life (estimated). fl is those that get life, fi is life that gets intelligent, fc is those that send signals, and L is how long they keep sending. Those last four are unknown.

That's why it's a model, not a prediction. It organizes what we know and what we don't.

24.text:
Where Is Everybody?

The Fermi paradox asks: if life is common, why have we found no sign of anyone else?

The galaxy is billions of years old. Even slow space travelers could have spread across it by now. Yet we see no sign of anyone. It's an open question.

Maybe life is rare. Maybe travel is too hard. Maybe civilizations don't last long. Or maybe we just haven't looked hard enough yet.

Did you know? Physicist Enrico Fermi asked "But where is everybody?" over lunch in 1950.

25.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 4

Two questions this time. First: why is the Drake equation a model, not a prediction? Is it A) most of its terms are unknown, so N could be 1 or millions, B) it was proven wrong by the Fermi paradox, C) it only works for our Solar System, or D) scientists have measured every term?

Second: which world vents its ocean into space, so a spacecraft can sample it without drilling? Is it A) Enceladus, B) Mars, C) Titan, or D) Proxima b?

26.text:
Our Cosmic Address, One More Line

Remember your cosmic address from Deck 1? Earth, Solar System, Milky Way, Universe. Now we add one more line: life?

Deck 1 showed where we are. Deck 19 showed where it all came from. Deck 20 asks: are we alone? The question mark is there on purpose. Nobody knows the answer yet. Maybe someday, someone in this class will help find it.

Write one sentence for each unit of the course, and one question you still want answered.

29.text:
The Standards Behind This Lesson

This lesson follows the Indiana Earth and Space Science standards. Here's what they ask, in plain words.

ES.2.2: describe the objects in the solar system, like planets, moons, comets, asteroids and protoplanets. Know that planets have been found orbiting other stars, and even drifting with no star at all. Describe how our solar system is organized. ES.1.1: explain how we study space by observing every kind of light with different telescopes and tools.

ES.2.1: make a flowchart showing how a solar system forms from a cloud, including stars, planetesimals, protoplanets, Jovian and terrestrial planets, moons and small bodies. ES.4.1: build a model of the gases in Earth's air, where they are and how they move, and show how the carbon and oxygen cycles swap gases with living things, oceans, rocks and industry.
